notes:
Here are verse-by-verse notes on Proverbs 16. Most of what I found comes from the older commentaries on biblehub.com, studylight.org and blueletterbible.org, and from David Guzik at enduringword.com. Some verses have little or no coverage, and a few gaps are listed at the end. Where I name a commentator's church tradition (Gill as a Particular Baptist, Clarke and Benson as Methodists, the Pulpit, Ellicott and Cambridge commentaries as Anglican, Keil–Delitzsch as Lutheran), that comes from my general knowledge. The pages themselves don't state it.

## 1. Traditional reading, verse by verse

**v. 1:** Guzik says people plan because they are made in God's image, and that when wisdom is given voice (the answer of the tongue), it is from the LORD – beyond the preparations of man's heart. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-16/
- Barnes: Thoughts come and go, as it were, spontaneously; but true, well ordered speech is the gift of God. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/proverbs/16-1.htm
- Several commentators point to Balaam, who meant to curse Israel but ended up blessing it. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/proverbs/16-1.htm
- Keil–Delitzsch: weighing a problem from every angle is man's work, but the fitting answer the tongue finally gives comes from God. Any preacher or writer facing a hard subject can confirm this. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/proverbs/16-1.htm

**v. 2:** Guzik: everyone instinctively justifies himself, but God weighs the spirit fairly and accurately. He quotes Spurgeon's remark that self-righteousness grows best where there seems to be the least ground for it. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-16/
- Matthew Henry: God not only sees men's ways but tries their spirits, and we are as our spirits are. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Pro/Pro_016.cfm

**v. 3:** The Hebrew for "commit" literally means "roll," as in rolling a burden onto someone else (Poole). Waltke: roll it onto the Lord and leave it there. Kidner: our plans stay our own, just less burdensome and better made. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-16/

**v. 4:** Kidner: there are no loose ends in God's world, and the verse does not make God the author of evil. Clarke: God doesn't make anyone wicked, but bears with those who make themselves so. Trapp denies that the verse teaches predestination to damnation. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-16/ (The traditions differ sharply here; see Part 2.)

**v. 5:** Guzik: God resists the proud. Even when the proud "join forces," as at Babel, they will not go unpunished. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-16/
- Henry: people can't punish pride, since they either admire it or fear it, so God punishes it himself. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Pro/Pro_016.cfm

**v. 6:** Guzik reads this as God's mercy and truth providing atonement, ultimately at the cross. He also notes Kidner's view that the mercy and faithfulness here are man's, as the fruit of repentance. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-16/ (Contested; see Part 2.)

**v. 7:** Guzik says the verse doesn't claim we can please God perfectly; it means a life that generally honours God. He cites Ross: such a life "disarms social hostility." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-16/
- Henry: God has access to every heart and can change enemies' minds. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Pro/Pro_016.cfm

**v. 8:** Guzik: great wealth without justice can't buy a clear conscience or the joy of God. The verse compares two options; it doesn't say they are the only ones. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-16/

**v. 9:** Guzik: planning is good, but every plan should be held humbly before God. He quotes Waltke: a man can't carry out his plan unless it fits Yahweh's plan for him. He also quotes Bridges: "man proposes, and God disposes." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-16/

**v. 10:** Guzik: "divination" here doesn't mean occult practice. It means wise, oracle-like judgment. He quotes Kidner: the Old Testament does not support the idea that the king can do no wrong (see Deuteronomy 17:18–20). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-16/

**v. 11:** Guzik cites Garrett: justice comes from God, Equity is not a human invention, and thus kings do not have the authority to suspend or violate the laws of fairness. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-16/

**v. 12:** Guzik: kings can do wickedness, and Solomon himself later did (1 Kings 11). Because a king has so much influence, his sin is all the worse. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-16/

**v. 13:** Guzik: leaders need honest counsel, not flattery. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-16/

**v. 14:** Guzik: a king's anger can mean death. He applies this to the King of Kings, whose wrath is appeased by what God provided in Christ, not by our merits. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-16/

**v. 15:** Guzik: the "latter rain" guaranteed a good harvest. The king's favour is life-giving in the same way, and even more so the favour of God's face (Numbers 6:25). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-16/

**v. 16:** Guzik: wisdom should be life's main pursuit. He adds that it also often leads to material prosperity as it did for Solomon. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-16/

**v. 17:** A Bible Hub study note: Walking in righteousness protects us from the snares of sin. https://biblehub.com/study/chapters/proverbs/16.htm

**v. 18:** Guzik links this to v. 5 and James 4:6: since God opposes the proud, it's no surprise that pride comes before destruction. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-16/

**v. 19:** Guzik: because pride leads to ruin, living humbly among the lowly is not so bad. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-16/

**v. 20:** Guzik (on "he who heeds the word wisely"): there are also foolish ways to heed God's word, like straining out a gnat and swallowing a camel. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/proverbs/proverbs-16.cfm
- Henry: some take "the word" to mean God's word. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Pro/Pro_016.cfm

**v. 22:** Henry on the second line: There is nothing that is good to be gotten by a fool. Even his instruction, his set and solemn discourses, are but folly. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Pro/Pro_016.cfm

**v. 23:** Henry: wisdom in the heart is what gives speech its weight. Clever phrasing may please the ear, but only real learning convinces. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Pro/Pro_016.cfm
- Guzik: our wisdom shows in what we say and how well we control our words. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/guzik_david/StudyGuide2017-Pro/Pro-16.cfm

**v. 25:** This repeats 14:12. Guzik says the repetition marks how important it is, and quotes an older writer: nothing is more common or more dangerous than self-delusion. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/proverbs/proverbs-16.cfm

**v. 26:** Guzik: when workers keep the fruit of their labour, they have a reason to work. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-16/

**vv. 27–30:** I found only a Bible Hub summary. It sees a dead end of self-reliance in vv. 25–27, and in vv. 28–30 Whisperers fracture friendships; violent plots hide behind winks and pursed lips. https://biblehub.com/study/chapters/proverbs/16.htm

**v. 31:** Henry: old people must hold on to their integrity for their grey hair to be a real crown, since Grace is the glory of old age. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Pro/Pro_016.cfm
- JFB: the sense may be that godliness is blessed with long life (compare 3:16). https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Pro/Pro_016.cfm

**v. 32:** Henry: Behold, a greater than Alexander or Caesar is here. Conquering your own passions takes more wisdom than winning a battle. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Pro/Pro_016.cfm

**v. 33:** Barnes: lots were thrown into the folds of a robe and drawn out. Where everything looked like pure chance, the Israelite teacher saw a higher will at work. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/proverbs/16-33.htm
- Waltke (quoted by Guzik) links this back to v. 32: in the end the Lord, not self-control alone, rules a person's destiny. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/proverbs/proverbs-16.cfm

## 2. Where Protestant traditions differ

**v. 4 (does God appoint the wicked to judgment?)**
- **Gill (Calvinist Baptist):** the verse is mainly about God's decrees; even the destruction of the wicked, which is under a divine appointment, is for his glory. He still insists God didn't make man in order to damn him. Man made himself wicked, and God may justly appoint him to damnation. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/proverbs/16-4.htm
- **Geneva Study Bible (Reformed):** God's justice will appear to his glory, even in the destruction of the wicked. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/proverbs/16-4.htm
- **Pulpit Commentary (Anglican):** says this clause has been perverted to support the terrible doctrine of reprobation. It cites 1 Timothy 2:4 and free will, and says punishment is prepared from God's foreknowledge of what people deserve. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/proverbs/16-4.htm
- **Ellicott (Anglican):** the verse does not mean that He created any one for punishment—i.e., predestined him for destruction. https://biblehub.com/proverbs/16-4.htm
- **Cambridge Bible:** what is revealed is "the righteous judgement of God," not arbitrary predestination. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/proverbs/16-4.htm
- **Clarke (Methodist):** God doesn't make the wicked, but bears with them; if they don't repent, wrath follows. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/proverbs/16-4.html
- **Keil–Delitzsch (Lutheran):** God made a being capable of wickedness, which then chose it. Even the wickedness of free agents is included in God's plan, so nothing people do takes him by surprise. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/proverbs/16-4.htm

**v. 6 (whose "mercy and truth" atones?)**
- **Gill:** it is God's mercy and truth, not man's. Kind deeds, truth-telling and alms will not atone for sin. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/proverbs/16-6.htm
- **Clarke:** God makes atonement through his mercy in sending Jesus. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/proverbs/16-6.html
- **Poole and Benson (Puritan and Methodist):** Poole says it is people's mercy and truth, which purge sin not meritoriously, but instrumentally, by preparing them to receive the pardon Christ bought. Benson says forgiveness and sanctification always go together. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/proverbs/16-6.htm
- **Cambridge Bible:** this isn't a statement of how atonement works. It moves a person's appropriation of atonement from ritual into moral life. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/proverbs/16-6.htm
- **Keil–Delitzsch:** Scripture gives good works a share in expiating sin "in a wider sense," as proof of grateful and compassionate love. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/proverbs/16-6.htm
- **Constable:** we don't atone for our own sin by being loving and truthful, but we should lovingly cover others' failings (1 Peter 4:8). https://www.studylight.org/commentary/proverbs/16-6.html

**v. 1 (is the heart's "preparation" man's or God's?)**
- **Henry, Benson and Gill**, following the KJV wording, take it to mean that all our ability to think and speak well comes from God. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/proverbs/16-1.htm
- **Clarke** argues that the Hebrew and the ancient versions make the plans man's. He adds that this doesn't mean anything good can come from the heart without God's influence. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/proverbs-16.html

**v. 33 (should Christians cast lots today?)**
- **Pulpit Commentary:** after the Spirit was poured out, the apostles never resorted to divination, and the Christian Church has wisely repudiated the practice. https://biblehub.com/proverbs/16-33.htm
- **Cambridge Bible:** religious use of the lot seems to have ended with Pentecost. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/proverbs/16-33.htm
- **Clarke** says he can't decide whether it is proper now. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/proverbs/16-33.html
- **Henry and Benson:** for weighty matters that can't be settled otherwise, lots may be used with prayer, and the result accepted. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/proverbs/16-33.htm
- **Keil–Delitzsch:** the verse is not a special endorsement of lots. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/proverbs/16-33.htm
- **Ligonier (Reformed devotional):** the verse covers even pagan or non-religious lots. It recalls R.C. Sproul's saying that there is no "maverick molecule." https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/lord-over-chance

## 3. Other views
- **Catholic reading of v. 6 (secondhand only):** Clarke quotes the Catholic commentator Calmet, who says we expiate sins through works of mercy and alms, and Clarke attacks him for it. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/proverbs-16.html I found no Catholic site giving its own view.
- **Ancient translations of v. 6:** the Pulpit Commentary notes that the Septuagint reads "By alms and faithfulness sins are cleansed." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/proverbs/16-6.htm The Vulgate uses "redimitur" ("is redeemed"). https://www.studylight.org/bible/lat/cvl/proverbs/16-6.html
- **Ancient translations of v. 4:** Clarke notes the Chaldee rendering, "All the works of the LORD are for those who obey him; and the wicked is reserved for the evil day." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/proverbs/16-4.html

**Not found:** NET Bible notes, Bible Odyssey, Orthodox or Catholic sites in their own words, and anything on prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace readings (for example of v. 3 or v. 7). I also found nothing specific on v. 21 or v. 24. I ran out of searches, so these would need another pass.
